PROP
41
PROHIBITS NEW STATE TAXES THAT EXCLUDE REVENUES FROM STATE SPENDING LIMIT. REQUIRES AUDITS FOR NEW STATE SPECIAL TAXES. INITIATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.
SUMMARY
Put on the Ballot by Petition Signatures
Nullifies state taxes enacted after January 1, 2026 that exempt their revenues from voter-approved state spending limit. Requires pre-election and recurring audits of programs funded by new special taxes. Fiscal Impact: The net fiscal effect is unknown as it depends on future decisions by voters, the Legislature, and other policymakers. Supporters: CA Society of Certified Public Accountants (CalCPAs); CalAsian Chamber of Commerce; California Taxpayers Association (CalTax) Opponents: US Senator Bernie Sanders; SEIU United Healthcare Workers West
WHAT YOUR VOTE MEANS
YES
A YES vote on this measure means: When special taxes are proposed by voter initiatives, the California State Auditor would review programs funded by the tax before the initiative appears on the ballot. The California State Auditor also would regularly review programs funded by special taxes approved by voters or the Legislature. In addition, the state might not be able to exclude any new special tax spending from its spending limit.
NO
A NO vote on this measure means: The California State Auditor’s responsibility to review government programs would not change. The state spending limit requirements would not change.
ARGUMENTS
PRO
Californians deserve better results for our taxes. Billions have flowed into programs like homelessness, with too little to show for it. Prop. 41 requires the independent State Auditor to conduct PUBLIC AUDITS of programs funded by new taxes—so we get more transparency, more accountability and better outcomes for taxpayers.
CON
Prop. 41 isn’t really about audits—it’s a billionaire-funded trick designed to undo the California Billionaire Tax. Billionaires would rather millions of Californians lose healthcare than pay a modest tax on their extreme wealth. Don’t fall for the billionaires’ lies. Vote NO on 41.

PROP
41
PROHIBITS NEW STATE TAXES THAT EXCLUDE REVENUES FROM STATE SPENDING LIMIT. REQUIRES AUDITS FOR NEW STATE SPECIAL TAXES. INITIATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.
SUMMARY
Put on the Ballot by Petition Signatures
Nullifies state taxes enacted after January 1, 2026 that exempt their revenues from voter-approved state spending limit. Requires pre-election and recurring audits of programs funded by new special taxes. Fiscal Impact: The net fiscal effect is unknown as it depends on future decisions by voters, the Legislature, and other policymakers. Supporters: CA Society of Certified Public Accountants (CalCPAs); CalAsian Chamber of Commerce; California Taxpayers Association (CalTax) Opponents: US Senator Bernie Sanders; SEIU United Healthcare Workers West
WHAT YOUR VOTE MEANS
YES
A YES vote on this measure means: When special taxes are proposed by voter initiatives, the California State Auditor would review programs funded by the tax before the initiative appears on the ballot. The California State Auditor also would regularly review programs funded by special taxes approved by voters or the Legislature. In addition, the state might not be able to exclude any new special tax spending from its spending limit.
NO
A NO vote on this measure means: The California State Auditor’s responsibility to review government programs would not change. The state spending limit requirements would not change.
ARGUMENTS
PRO
Californians deserve better results for our taxes. Billions have flowed into programs like homelessness, with too little to show for it. Prop. 41 requires the independent State Auditor to conduct PUBLIC AUDITS of programs funded by new taxes—so we get more transparency, more accountability and better outcomes for taxpayers.
CON
Prop. 41 isn’t really about audits—it’s a billionaire-funded trick designed to undo the California Billionaire Tax. Billionaires would rather millions of Californians lose healthcare than pay a modest tax on their extreme wealth. Don’t fall for the billionaires’ lies. Vote NO on 41.

- NY Post (Oct 29): Kalshi 54%, Polymarket 59% for Prop 41 passage

Voters Are Displeased by Long Ballots and Split on Ballot Propositions
Stephanie Barton (https://www.ppic.org/person/stephanie-barton/)
Subscribe to our blog → (https://www.ppic.org/mailing-list)
View Larger (javascript:void(0))
Stephanie Barton (https://www.ppic.org/person/stephanie-barton/)
Stephanie Barton (https://www.ppic.org/person/stephanie-barton/)
The November 3 ballot will ask Californians to choose their next governor and decide on over a dozen measures, a number of ballot measures that many deem excessive. At a recent event, survey analyst Deja Thomas shared findings from the latest PPIC Statewide Survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), outlining support for gubernatorial candidates, opinions on the number of ballot measures and their language as well as views on the direction of the state and nation.
In the governor’s race, Xavier Becerra maintains a lead over Steve Hilton: 6 in 10 likely voters support Becerra while nearly 4 in 10 support Hilton. Except for a slim majority in the Central Valley who favor Hilton, majorities of likely voters across demographic groups and regions favor Becerra. For House races in the midterm, about 6 in10 likely voters would vote for the Democratic candidate and just over a third would vote for the Republican.
To offer insight into some competitive House races, Thomas turned to regional findings. In the Central Valley, home of two competitive districts, 51% of likely voters prefer the Republican candidate; those in the Inland Empire and Orange/San Diego prefer the Democratic candidate.
The 14 propositions on the upcoming ballot represent the highest number since the November 2016 election. Along with agreeing that ballots are too long, likely voters agree that the wording for citizens’ initiatives is too complicated, which makes it confusing to understand what happens if an initiative passes.
Thomas discussed findings for Proposition 40 in greater detail; if passed, it would impose a one-time 5% tax on taxpayers with assets over $1 billion. A thin majority (52%) of likely voters would vote yes and 46% would vote no. A measure that would make an existing tax on higher incomes (over 371K) permanent, Proposition 3, earned greater support than Proposition 40: 58% would vote yes and 40% would vote no.
Measures that could nullify Proposition 40 also get slim support: 51% of likely voters would vote yes on Proposition 41, and 54% would vote yes on Proposition 42, a comparison that surprised Thomas. Proposition 41 would require the state auditor to approve new special taxes, and Proposition 42 would restrict new taxes on personal property.
Voters will weigh in on these measures at a time when about 7 in 10 Californians expect bad economic times ahead for the state, an opinion a majority has held since 2022, according to Thomas. Pessimism about the direction of the country is 10 points higher than before the 2024 presidential election, with 8 in 10 now saying things are going the wrong way.
Concerns with affordability may be driving this sour attitude, and it was a key theme in the survey. “In the governor’s race, most Becerra and Hilton supporters hold negative outlooks of the state’s economy, but Hilton supporters are far more likely to say this,” Thomas said, adding that 65% of likely voters consider a candidate’s position on affordability very important to their vote. “It will be a key issue on election day.”

Blog Post · September 24, 2026
Voters Are Displeased by Long Ballots and Split on Ballot Propositions
Stephanie Barton (https://www.ppic.org/person/stephanie-barton/)
Subscribe to our blog → (https://www.ppic.org/mailing-list)
View Larger (javascript:void(0))
Stephanie Barton (https://www.ppic.org/person/stephanie-barton/)
Stephanie Barton (https://www.ppic.org/person/stephanie-barton/)
The November 3 ballot will ask Californians to choose their next governor and decide on over a dozen measures, a number of ballot measures that many deem excessive. At a recent event, survey analyst Deja Thomas shared findings from the latest PPIC Statewide Survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), outlining support for gubernatorial candidates, opinions on the number of ballot measures and their language as well as views on the direction of the state and nation.
In the governor’s race, Xavier Becerra maintains a lead over Steve Hilton: 6 in 10 likely voters support Becerra while nearly 4 in 10 support Hilton. Except for a slim majority in the Central Valley who favor Hilton, majorities of likely voters across demographic groups and regions favor Becerra. For House races in the midterm, about 6 in10 likely voters would vote for the Democratic candidate and just over a third would vote for the Republican.
To offer insight into some competitive House races, Thomas turned to regional findings. In the Central Valley, home of two competitive districts, 51% of likely voters prefer the Republican candidate; those in the Inland Empire and Orange/San Diego prefer the Democratic candidate.
The 14 propositions on the upcoming ballot represent the highest number since the November 2016 election. Along with agreeing that ballots are too long, likely voters agree that the wording for citizens’ initiatives is too complicated, which makes it confusing to understand what happens if an initiative passes.
Thomas discussed findings for Proposition 40 in greater detail; if passed, it would impose a one-time 5% tax on taxpayers with assets over $1 billion. A thin majority (52%) of likely voters would vote yes and 46% would vote no. A measure that would make an existing tax on higher incomes (over 371K) permanent, Proposition 3, earned greater support than Proposition 40: 58% would vote yes and 40% would vote no.
Measures that could nullify Proposition 40 also get slim support: 51% of likely voters would vote yes on Proposition 41, and 54% would vote yes on Proposition 42, a comparison that surprised Thomas. Proposition 41 would require the state auditor to approve new special taxes, and Proposition 42 would restrict new taxes on personal property.
Voters will weigh in on these measures at a time when about 7 in 10 Californians expect bad economic times ahead for the state, an opinion a majority has held since 2022, according to Thomas. Pessimism about the direction of the country is 10 points higher than before the 2024 presidential election, with 8 in 10 now saying things are going the wrong way.
Concerns with affordability may be driving this sour attitude, and it was a key theme in the survey. “In the governor’s race, most Becerra and Hilton supporters hold negative outlooks of the state’s economy, but Hilton supporters are far more likely to say this,” Thomas said, adding that 65% of likely voters consider a candidate’s position on affordability very important to their vote. “It will be a key issue on election day.”

Blog Post · September 24, 2026
Voters Are Displeased by Long Ballots and Split on Ballot Propositions
Stephanie Barton (https://www.ppic.org/person/stephanie-barton/)
Subscribe to our blog → (https://www.ppic.org/mailing-list)
View Larger (javascript:void(0))
Stephanie Barton (https://www.ppic.org/person/stephanie-barton/)
Stephanie Barton (https://www.ppic.org/person/stephanie-barton/)
The November 3 ballot will ask Californians to choose their next governor and decide on over a dozen measures, a number of ballot measures that many deem excessive. At a recent event, survey analyst Deja Thomas shared findings from the latest PPIC Statewide Survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), outlining support for gubernatorial candidates, opinions on the number of ballot measures and their language as well as views on the direction of the state and nation.
In the governor’s race, Xavier Becerra maintains a lead over Steve Hilton: 6 in 10 likely voters support Becerra while nearly 4 in 10 support Hilton. Except for a slim majority in the Central Valley who favor Hilton, majorities of likely voters across demographic groups and regions favor Becerra. For House races in the midterm, about 6 in10 likely voters would vote for the Democratic candidate and just over a third would vote for the Republican.
To offer insight into some competitive House races, Thomas turned to regional findings. In the Central Valley, home of two competitive districts, 51% of likely voters prefer the Republican candidate; those in the Inland Empire and Orange/San Diego prefer the Democratic candidate.
The 14 propositions on the upcoming ballot represent the highest number since the November 2016 election. Along with agreeing that ballots are too long, likely voters agree that the wording for citizens’ initiatives is too complicated, which makes it confusing to understand what happens if an initiative passes.
Thomas discussed findings for Proposition 40 in greater detail; if passed, it would impose a one-time 5% tax on taxpayers with assets over $1 billion. A thin majority (52%) of likely voters would vote yes and 46% would vote no. A measure that would make an existing tax on higher incomes (over 371K) permanent, Proposition 3, earned greater support than Proposition 40: 58% would vote yes and 40% would vote no.
Measures that could nullify Proposition 40 also get slim support: 51% of likely voters would vote yes on Proposition 41, and 54% would vote yes on Proposition 42, a comparison that surprised Thomas. Proposition 41 would require the state auditor to approve new special taxes, and Proposition 42 would restrict new taxes on personal property.
Voters will weigh in on these measures at a time when about 7 in 10 Californians expect bad economic times ahead for the state, an opinion a majority has held since 2022, according to Thomas. Pessimism about the direction of the country is 10 points higher than before the 2024 presidential election, with 8 in 10 now saying things are going the wrong way.
Concerns with affordability may be driving this sour attitude, and it was a key theme in the survey. “In the governor’s race, most Becerra and Hilton supporters hold negative outlooks of the state’s economy, but Hilton supporters are far more likely to say this,” Thomas said, adding that 65% of likely voters consider a candidate’s position on affordability very important to their vote. “It will be a key issue on election day.”

Interesting — the prediction markets are split. Let me gather the data:

**Polling for Prop 41:**
- Berkeley IGS (Aug 3-9): No +2 (37% No, 35% Yes)
- PPIC (Sept 4-10): 51% Yes (51% support)
- Berkeley IGS (Sept 15-20): Yes +4 (37% Yes, 33% No)
- IVC Media (Sept 23-28): Yes +13 (49% Yes, 36% No)
- PPIC (Oct 16-22): No +1 (48% Yes, 49% No) — essentially tied
- Berkeley IGS (Oct 19-25): No +9 (47% No, 38% Yes)

**Prediction markets (as of ~Nov 1-3, 2026):**
- Kalshi: 42.5% chance of passage (as of Nov 3, 12:11 AM ET) — declined 9.5 points in 24h, 7 points over 7 days
- Polymarket: 66% chance of passage (per Nijinn) / 67% (per Polymarket page) — but very low volume ($1.9K traded), so unreliable
- NY Post (Oct 29): Kalshi 54%, Polymarket 59% for Prop 41 passage

Hmm, there's a conflict: the polling shows No leading, but prediction markets (as of Oct 29) showed Yes favored at 54-59%. But by Nov 3, Kalshi dropped to 42.5% (below 50), while Polymarket stayed at 66-67% (but with tiny volume).

Wait, there's something odd about the Polymarket market: "Not counted: bid and ask more than 10 pts apart · bid 43.0% / ask 89.0%". So the Polymarket market is illiquid. The $1.9K volume is negligible. The Kalshi market at 42.5% as of Nov 3, 12:11 AM ET suggests the Yes side is now slightly favored to LOSE.

Also, the NY Post article from Oct 29 said Kalshi: 54% | Polymarket: 59% for Prop 41. Then Nijinn's data shows Kalshi at 42.5% as of Nov 3 12:11 AM ET, having dropped 9.5 points in 24h. That's a big drop — possibly due to late polling or early vote data.

Hmm wait, but the current date. Let me think about what today's date is. The user's question is being asked presumably before the election. The Nijinn data says "Updated Nov 3, 2026, 12:11 AM ET". The East Bay Times editorial is dated Nov 2. So the current date is likely Nov 2 or Nov 3, 2026, i.e., right before or on Election Day.

Actually, since this appears to be a real-time question about an ongoing election, the answer depends on the best available evidence right now.

Let me weigh the evidence:

**For No (defeat):**
1. Two high-quality late-October polls both show No leading:
   - PPIC Oct 16-22: 48% Yes, 49% No
   - Berkeley IGS Oct 19-25: 38% Yes, 47% No (No +9)
2. IGS trend: Sept (Yes+4) → Oct (No+9) — significant deterioration
3. PPIC trend: Sept (51% Yes) → Oct (48% Yes) — declining
4. Undecided voters (15-16% in IGS) historically break toward No on California initiatives
5. Major editorial opposition (LA Times, SF Chronicle, etc. — the No on 41 campaign got editorial endorsements)
6. Democratic Party and labor unions oppose it — California is a heavily Democratic state
7. The "billionaire-funded trick" framing has resonated
8. Kalshi dropped to 42.5% by Nov 3 (below 50%)

**For Yes (passage):**
1. The Yes side massively outspent the No side on Prop 41 ($58.4M vs $22.7M), funded by billionaires
2. Some prediction markets (Polymarket, low volume) show ~66% chance of passage
3. NY Post Oct 29: Kalshi 54%, Polymarket 59%
4. The ballot title/summary sounds appealing (audits, accountability, transparency)
5. IVC Media poll (Sept 23-28) showed Yes +13

Hmm, the evidence is genuinely mixed, but I think the weight favors No:
- The two most recent, most reliable polls (PPIC and Berkeley IGS) both show No leading, with the IGS showing No +9
- Support has been trending down consistently
- Undecideds break No
- The final Kalshi price (42.5% as of Nov 3) — closest to election — favors No

Actually, wait. I should be careful about the Kalshi price. Nijinn shows "42.5% chance it passes... Kalshi only... Updated Nov 3, 2026, 12:11 AM ET". And "24h −9.5" means it dropped 9.5 points in the last 24 hours. That's a substantial late movement toward No.

Also the Polymarket market at 66% has only $1,925 volume — essentially no liquidity, and the bid/ask spread (43.0%/89.0%) is huge, meaning the "last trade" price is not meaningful. Actually the spread listed as bid 43/ask 89 suggests the market is basically unpriced.

Hmm, but the NY Post article from Oct 29 says Polymarket 59%. And the Polymarket page fetched now says 67% chance / 90% for Yes in one place. These are contradictory. The Polymarket data seems unreliable due to low volume.

Let me check the Kalshi market directly for the latest odds. Also, let me look for any very late polling or exit poll data. And let me verify the PPIC October poll numbers directly.

Also, I should consider: are there any more recent polls (Emerson, SurveyUSA, etc.)? Let me search.

Blog Post · September 24, 2026
Voters Are Displeased by Long Ballots and Split on Ballot Propositions
Stephanie Barton (https://www.ppic.org/person/stephanie-barton/)
Subscribe to our blog → (https://www.ppic.org/mailing-list)
View Larger (javascript:void(0))
Stephanie Barton (https://www.ppic.org/person/stephanie-barton/)
Stephanie Barton (https://www.ppic.org/person/stephanie-barton/)
The November 3 ballot will ask Californians to choose their next governor and decide on over a dozen measures, a number of ballot measures that many deem excessive. At a recent event, survey analyst Deja Thomas shared findings from the latest PPIC Statewide Survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), outlining support for gubernatorial candidates, opinions on the number of ballot measures and their language as well as views on the direction of the state and nation.
In the governor’s race, Xavier Becerra maintains a lead over Steve Hilton: 6 in 10 likely voters support Becerra while nearly 4 in 10 support Hilton. Except for a slim majority in the Central Valley who favor Hilton, majorities of likely voters across demographic groups and regions favor Becerra. For House races in the midterm, about 6 in10 likely voters would vote for the Democratic candidate and just over a third would vote for the Republican.
To offer insight into some competitive House races, Thomas turned to regional findings. In the Central Valley, home of two competitive districts, 51% of likely voters prefer the Republican candidate; those in the Inland Empire and Orange/San Diego prefer the Democratic candidate.
The 14 propositions on the upcoming ballot represent the highest number since the November 2016 election. Along with agreeing that ballots are too long, likely voters agree that the wording for citizens’ initiatives is too complicated, which makes it confusing to understand what happens if an initiative passes.
Thomas discussed findings for Proposition 40 in greater detail; if passed, it would impose a one-time 5% tax on taxpayers with assets over $1 billion. A thin majority (52%) of likely voters would vote yes and 46% would vote no. A measure that would make an existing tax on higher incomes (over 371K) permanent, Proposition 3, earned greater support than Proposition 40: 58% would vote yes and 40% would vote no.
Measures that could nullify Proposition 40 also get slim support: 51% of likely voters would vote yes on Proposition 41, and 54% would vote yes on Proposition 42, a comparison that surprised Thomas. Proposition 41 would require the state auditor to approve new special taxes, and Proposition 42 would restrict new taxes on personal property.
Voters will weigh in on these measures at a time when about 7 in 10 Californians expect bad economic times ahead for the state, an opinion a majority has held since 2022, according to Thomas. Pessimism about the direction of the country is 10 points higher than before the 2024 presidential election, with 8 in 10 now saying things are going the wrong way.
Concerns with affordability may be driving this sour attitude, and it was a key theme in the survey. “In the governor’s race, most Becerra and Hilton supporters hold negative outlooks of the state’s economy, but Hilton supporters are far more likely to say this,” Thomas said, adding that 65% of likely voters consider a candidate’s position on affordability very important to their vote. “It will be a key issue on election day.”

assistantMessageEvent.content:
Now I have a much clearer picture. Let me compile everything:

**Latest Kalshi odds (as of Nov 3, 2026, 12:11 AM ET, i.e., essentially Election Eve):**
- Proposition 41: 42% chance of passage (Yes 46¢, No 63¢... wait, that's odd. Yes 46¢ = 46%, No 63¢ = 63%. Hmm, they don't sum to 100 due to the spread. The headline says "42%" chance.)
- The Kalshi market dropped ~9.5 points in the last 24 hours
- Nijinn TruthIndex: 42.5% chance of passage (Kalshi only)
- On Point Politics forecast: Prop 41 "favored to fail" — Yes at 46.4%, only 20.4% chance to pass in their simulations
- NY Post (Oct 29): Kalshi 54% | Polymarket 59% — but this was several days before, and Kalshi has since dropped to ~42%
- Polymarket: ~66% Yes but with only $1,925 volume and huge bid/ask spread — unreliable, essentially illiquid

**Polling summary:**
| Poll | Dates | Yes | No | Result |
|------|-------|-----|-----|--------|
| Berkeley IGS | Aug 3-9 | 35% | 37% | No +2 |
| PPIC | Sept 4-10 | 51% | — | Yes leading |
| Berkeley IGS | Sept 15-20 | 37% | 33% | Yes +4 |
| IVC Media | Sept 23-28 | 49% | 36% | Yes +13 |
| PPIC | Oct 16-22 | 48% | 49% | No +1 (tied) |
| Berkeley IGS | Oct 19-25 | 38% | 47% | No +9 |

The trend is clearly deteriorating for Yes. Both of the final polls from the two most reputable California pollsters (PPIC and Berkeley IGS) show No leading.

**Key dynamics:**
1. The No side (SEIU-UHW, California Democratic Party, labor) has successfully framed Prop 41 as a "billionaire-funded trick" to undo the billionaire tax (Prop 40).
2. Major editorial boards oppose it.
3. California is a deep blue state where the Democratic Party and unions have strong messaging infrastructure.
4. Undecided voters (15-16% in the final IGS poll) typically break toward No on ballot initiatives.
5. Prediction markets have moved sharply toward No in the final days (Kalshi from 54% on Oct 29 to 42% by Nov 3).

**Counter-considerations:**
1. The Yes side has vastly more money ($58.4M vs $22.7M on Prop 41 specifically).
2. The ballot title sounds appealing (audits, accountability).
3. Prop 42 (the companion measure) has slightly better polling (51% yes in PPIC Oct).
4. Polymarket still shows ~66% Yes, but it's illiquid.

Weighing everything: The most reliable evidence — two independent, high-quality final polls showing No leading (especially Berkeley IGS at No +9), the sharp late movement in the Kalshi market toward No, and the On Point Politics forecast model giving Yes only a 20% chance — all point to the **No side being more likely to win**.

The polling average is around 43-46% Yes, which is below the 50% needed, and undecideds break toward No.

So the answer to "Which side is more likely to win?" is the No side → answer "no".

Let me do one more check on the very latest news to make sure I'm not missing anything (e.g., final weekend polls, early voting data).
Let me check the most recent news and the On Point Politics forecast for final confirmation.

- Proposition 41: 42% chance of passage (Yes 46¢, No 63¢... wait, that's odd. Yes 46¢ = 46%, No 63¢ = 63%. Hmm, they don't sum to 100 due to the spread. The headline says "42%" chance.)
- The Kalshi market dropped ~9.5 points in the last 24 hours
- Nijinn TruthIndex: 42.5% chance of passage (Kalshi only)
- On Point Politics forecast: Prop 41 "favored to fail" — Yes at 46.4%, only 20.4% chance to pass in their simulations
- NY Post (Oct 29): Kalshi 54% | Polymarket 59% — but this was several days before, and Kalshi has since dropped to ~42%
- Polymarket: ~66% Yes but with only $1,925 volume and huge bid/ask spread — unreliable, essentially illiquid

**Polling summary:**
| Poll | Dates | Yes | No | Result |
|------|-------|-----|-----|--------|
| Berkeley IGS | Aug 3-9 | 35% | 37% | No +2 |
| PPIC | Sept 4-10 | 51% | — | Yes leading |
| Berkeley IGS | Sept 15-20 | 37% | 33% | Yes +4 |
| IVC Media | Sept 23-28 | 49% | 36% | Yes +13 |
| PPIC | Oct 16-22 | 48% | 49% | No +1 (tied) |
| Berkeley IGS | Oct 19-25 | 38% | 47% | No +9 |

The trend is clearly deteriorating for Yes. Both of the final polls from the two most reputable California pollsters (PPIC and Berkeley IGS) show No leading.

**Key dynamics:**
1. The No side (SEIU-UHW, California Democratic Party, labor) has successfully framed Prop 41 as a "billionaire-funded trick" to undo the billionaire tax (Prop 40).
2. Major editorial boards oppose it.
3. California is a deep blue state where the Democratic Party and unions have strong messaging infrastructure.
4. Undecided voters (15-16% in the final IGS poll) typically break toward No on ballot initiatives.
5. Prediction markets have moved sharply toward No in the final days (Kalshi from 54% on Oct 29 to 42% by Nov 3).

**Counter-considerations:**
1. The Yes side has vastly more money ($58.4M vs $22.7M on Prop 41 specifically).
2. The ballot title sounds appealing (audits, accountability).
3. Prop 42 (the companion measure) has slightly better polling (51% yes in PPIC Oct).
4. Polymarket still shows ~66% Yes, but it's illiquid.

Weighing everything: The most reliable evidence — two independent, high-quality final polls showing No leading (especially Berkeley IGS at No +9), the sharp late movement in the Kalshi market toward No, and the On Point Politics forecast model giving Yes only a 20% chance — all point to the **No side being more likely to win**.

The polling average is around 43-46% Yes, which is below the 50% needed, and undecideds break toward No.

So the answer to "Which side is more likely to win?" is the No side → answer "no".

Let me do one more check on the very latest news to make sure I'm not missing anything (e.g., final weekend polls, early voting data).","format":"unknown","index":0}]

A pair of statewide measures aimed at blocking Proposition 40, Proposition 41 and Proposition 42, remained short of the needed majority support, with opposition mounting, the poll found.
Proposition 41 had support from 38% of likely voters while 47% were opposed and 16% were undecided, compared to IGS’ mid-September poll in which 37% were in favor, 33% opposed and 30% undecided.
Proposition 42 support remained at 43% as it was in September, while opposition rose to 45% from 34% and undecided fell to 12% from 23% last month.
Both also require majorities to pass.
If either passes and receives more “yes” votes than Proposition 40, it could prevent the wealth tax from taking effect if courts find the measures conflict.

How this is built
Proposition 41 is forecast as a other taxes measure whose Yes vote leans Republican . Now I have a much clearer picture. Let me compile everything:

**Latest Kalshi odds (as of Nov 3, 2026, 12:11 AM ET, i.e., essentially Election Eve):**
- Proposition 41: 42% chance of passage (Yes 46¢, No 63¢... wait, that's odd. Yes 46¢ = 46%, No 63¢ = 63%. Hmm, they don't sum to 100 due to the spread. The headline says "42%" chance.)
- The Kalshi market dropped ~9.5 points in the last 24 hours
- Nijinn TruthIndex: 42.5% chance of passage (Kalshi only)
- On Point Politics forecast: Prop 41 "favored to fail" — Yes at 46.4%, only 20.4% chance to pass in their simulations
- NY Post (Oct 29): Kalshi 54% | Polymarket 59% — but this was several days before, and Kalshi has since dropped to ~42%
- Polymarket: ~66% Yes but with only $1,925 volume and huge bid/ask spread — unreliable, essentially illiquid

**Polling summary:**
| Poll | Dates | Yes | No | Result |
|------|-------|-----|-----|--------|
| Berkeley IGS | Aug 3-9 | 35% | 37% | No +2 |
| PPIC | Sept 4-10 | 51% | — | Yes leading |
| Berkeley IGS | Sept 15-20 | 37% | 33% | Yes +4 |
| IVC Media | Sept 23-28 | 49% | 36% | Yes +13 |
| PPIC | Oct 16-22 | 48% | 49% | No +1 (tied) |
| Berkeley IGS | Oct 19-25 | 38% | 47% | No +9 |

The trend is clearly deteriorating for Yes. Both of the final polls from the two most reputable California pollsters (PPIC and Berkeley IGS) show No leading.

**Key dynamics:**
1. The No side (SEIU-UHW, California Democratic Party, labor) has successfully framed Prop 41 as a "billionaire-funded trick" to undo the billionaire tax (Prop 40).
2. Major editorial boards oppose it.
3. California is a deep blue state where the Democratic Party and unions have strong messaging infrastructure.
4. Undecided voters (15-16% in the final IGS poll) typically break toward No on ballot initiatives.
5. Prediction markets have moved sharply toward No in the final days (Kalshi from 54% on Oct 29 to 42% by Nov 3).

**Counter-considerations:**

The polling average is around 43-46% Yes, which is below the 50% needed, and undecideds break toward No.

So the answer to "Which side is more likely to win?" is the No side → answer "no".

Now I have a comprehensive picture. Let me summarize all the evidence for Proposition 41 (California, November 3, 2026 election):

**Polling (all public polls):**
1. Berkeley IGS (Aug 3-9): Yes 35%, No 37% — No +2
2. PPIC (Sept 4-10): Yes 51%, No 44% — Yes +7
3. Berkeley IGS (Sept 15-20): Yes 37%, No 33% — Yes +4 (30% undecided)
4. PPIC (Oct 16-22): Yes 48%, No 49% — No +1 (essentially tied)
5. Berkeley IGS (Oct 19-25): Yes 38%, No 47% — No +9 (16% undecided)

Trend: Yes support has declined from 51% (Sept PPIC) to 48%/38% in late October. Both final polls show No leading. Polling average (On Point): 46.6% Yes.

**Forecasts and prediction markets:**
- On Point Politics (Nov 2): Yes has only 20.4% chance to pass; forecast Yes 46.4% vs No 53.6%. "Proposition 41 is favored to fail."
- Kalshi (Nov 3, 12:11 AM ET): ~42-42.5% chance of passage, having dropped 9.5 points in the last 24 hours and 7 points over 7 days
- NY Post (Oct 29): Kalshi 54%, Polymarket 59% — but these have since moved down on Kalshi
- Polymarket: ~66% Yes but with only $1,925 in volume and a huge bid/ask spread (43%/89%) — illiquid and unreliable

**Other factors favoring No:**
- Undecided voters (15-16%) typically break 2:1 toward No on ballot initiatives
- The No campaign (SEIU-UHW, California Democratic Party, labor unions, Bernie Sanders) has framed it effectively as a "billionaire-funded trick"
- California is a deep-blue state; the measure's Yes vote "leans Republican" per On Point Politics
- Editorial boards (Mercury News, East Bay Times, LA Times, SF Chronicle) oppose it
- Support has been consistently declining through October as the opposition message lands

**Factors favoring Yes:**
- Massive spending advantage: $58.4M raised for Yes vs. $22.7M for No on Prop 41 specifically (billionaire-funded via Building a Better California, $103M spent supporting Prop 41)
- The ballot title/summary sounds appealing (audits, transparency, accountability)
- PPIC's October poll has it essentially tied (48-49)
- Prop 42 (companion) at 51% in PPIC October poll

**Weighing the evidence:**
The preponderance of evidence points to the No side being more likely to win:
1. Both final independent polls (PPIC Oct 16-22 and Berkeley IGS Oct 19-25) show No ahead
2. Clear downward trend in Yes support through the fall
3. Undecideds break toward No
4. The On Point Politics simulation model gives Yes just a 20.4% chance
5. Kalshi's final price (~42%) is below 50%, with sharp late movement toward No
6. Structural factors: Democratic-leaning electorate, measure's coalition leans Republican, strong editorial and party opposition

The one dissenting signal is the illiquid Polymarket market (~66% Yes, $1.9K volume), which is not credible given the tiny volume and wide spread. Also, the NY Post Oct 29 numbers (Kalshi 54%) were a few days older and Kalshi subsequently dropped ~12 points.

Note: One Mercury News article quotes the Yes campaign claiming "Recent polling shows that 58% support the concept of Prop 41" — this appears to be campaign spin about the "concept" (audits/accountability) rather than the actual ballot question.

So my conclusion: The **No** side is more likely to win. The answer to "Which side is more likely to win?" is "no" (i.e., the No side / the proposition is more likely to be defeated).

I now have a comprehensive picture. Let me summarize my research:

**Proposition 41 (California, Nov. 3, 2026 ballot):** A billionaire-funded counter-measure to Prop 40 (the "billionaire tax") that would prohibit new state taxes exempted from the spending limit and require audits of new special taxes. Yes = pass the measure; No = defeat it.

**Polling evidence (all public polls):**
- Berkeley IGS (Aug): Yes 35% / No 37%
- PPIC (Sept): Yes 51% / No 44%
- Berkeley IGS (mid-Sept): Yes 37% / No 33% (30% undecided)
- PPIC (Oct 16–22): Yes 48% / No 49% — tied/tilted No
- Berkeley IGS (Oct 19–25): Yes 38% / No 47% — No +9, with 16% undecided

Both final, high-quality polls show the No side ahead, and Yes support has steadily eroded through October as the "billionaire-funded trick" message landed.

**Forecasts & markets:**
- On Point Politics model (Nov 2): Yes at 46.4%, only a **20.4% chance to pass** — "favored to fail"
- Kalshi (Election Eve): ~42% chance of passage, having dropped ~9.5 points in the final 24 hours
- Polymarket showed ~66% Yes, but with only ~$1.9K volume and a 43¢/89¢ bid-ask spread — too illiquid to be meaningful

**Other factors:** Undecided voters historically break toward No on California initiatives; the Democratic Party, labor unions, and major editorial boards all oppose it in a deep-blue state; and the Yes coalition leans Republican in a Democratic-trending midterm electorate. The Yes side's massive spending advantage ($58M vs. $23M) hasn't stopped the slide.

The weight of evidence — both final polls showing No ahead, a deteriorating trend, undecideds breaking No, a forecast model giving Yes only ~20%, and Kalshi falling below 50% — indicates the **No side** is more likely to win.

PROP
41
PROHIBITS NEW STATE TAXES THAT EXCLUDE REVENUES FROM STATE SPENDING LIMIT. REQUIRES AUDITS FOR NEW STATE SPECIAL TAXES. INITIATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.
SUMMARY
Put on the Ballot by Petition Signatures
Nullifies state taxes enacted after January 1, 2026 that exempt their revenues from voter-approved state spending limit. Requires pre-election and recurring audits of programs funded by new special taxes. Fiscal Impact: The net fiscal effect is unknown as it depends on future decisions by voters, the Legislature, and other policymakers. Supporters: CA Society of Certified Public Accountants (CalCPAs); CalAsian Chamber of Commerce; California Taxpayers Association (CalTax) Opponents: US Senator Bernie Sanders; SEIU United Healthcare Workers West
WHAT YOUR VOTE MEANS
YES
A YES vote on this measure means: When special taxes are proposed by voter initiatives, the California State Auditor would review programs funded by the tax before the initiative appears on the ballot. The California State Auditor also would regularly review programs funded by special taxes approved by voters or the Legislature. In addition, the state might not be able to exclude any new special tax spending from its spending limit.
NO
A NO vote on this measure means: The California State Auditor’s responsibility to review government programs would not change. The state spending limit requirements would not change.
ARGUMENTS
PRO
Californians deserve better results for our taxes. Billions have flowed into programs like homelessness, with too little to show for it. Prop. 41 requires the independent State Auditor to conduct PUBLIC AUDITS of programs funded by new taxes—so we get more transparency, more accountability and better outcomes for taxpayers.
CON
Prop. 41 isn’t really about audits—it’s a billionaire-funded trick designed to undo the California Billionaire Tax. Billionaires would rather millions of Californians lose healthcare than pay a modest tax on their extreme wealth. Don’t fall for the billionaires’ lies. Vote NO on 41.

Voters Are Displeased by Long Ballots and Split on Ballot Propositions
Stephanie Barton (https://www.ppic.org/person/stephanie-barton/)
Subscribe to our blog → (https://www.ppic.org/mailing-list)
View Larger (javascript:void(0))
Stephanie Barton (https://www.ppic.org/person/stephanie-barton/)
Stephanie Barton (https://www.ppic.org/person/stephanie-barton/)
The November 3 ballot will ask Californians to choose their next governor and decide on over a dozen measures, a number of ballot measures that many deem excessive. At a recent event, survey analyst Deja Thomas shared findings from the latest PPIC Statewide Survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), outlining support for gubernatorial candidates, opinions on the number of ballot measures and their language as well as views on the direction of the state and nation.
In the governor’s race, Xavier Becerra maintains a lead over Steve Hilton: 6 in 10 likely voters support Becerra while nearly 4 in 10 support Hilton. Except for a slim majority in the Central Valley who favor Hilton, majorities of likely voters across demographic groups and regions favor Becerra. For House races in the midterm, about 6 in10 likely voters would vote for the Democratic candidate and just over a third would vote for the Republican.
To offer insight into some competitive House races, Thomas turned to regional findings. In the Central Valley, home of two competitive districts, 51% of likely voters prefer the Republican candidate; those in the Inland Empire and Orange/San Diego prefer the Democratic candidate.
The 14 propositions on the upcoming ballot represent the highest number since the November 2016 election. Along with agreeing that ballots are too long, likely voters agree that the wording for citizens’ initiatives is too complicated, which makes it confusing to understand what happens if an initiative passes.
Thomas discussed findings for Proposition 40 in greater detail; if passed, it would impose a one-time 5% tax on taxpayers with assets over $1 billion. A thin majority (52%) of likely voters would vote yes and 46% would vote no. A measure that would make an existing tax on higher incomes (over 371K) permanent, Proposition 3, earned greater support than Proposition 40: 58% would vote yes and 40% would vote no.
Measures that could nullify Proposition 40 also get slim support: 51% of likely voters would vote yes on Proposition 41, and 54% would vote yes on Proposition 42, a comparison that surprised Thomas. Proposition 41 would require the state auditor to approve new special taxes, and Proposition 42 would restrict new taxes on personal property.
Voters will weigh in on these measures at a time when about 7 in 10 Californians expect bad economic times ahead for the state, an opinion a majority has held since 2022, according to Thomas. Pessimism about the direction of the country is 10 points higher than before the 2024 presidential election, with 8 in 10 now saying things are going the wrong way.
Concerns with affordability may be driving this sour attitude, and it was a key theme in the survey. “In the governor’s race, most Becerra and Hilton supporters hold negative outlooks of the state’s economy, but Hilton supporters are far more likely to say this,” Thomas said, adding that 65% of likely voters consider a candidate’s position on affordability very important to their vote. “It will be a key issue on election day.”

Now I have a much clearer picture. Let me compile everything:

**Latest Kalshi odds (as of Nov 3, 2026, 12:11 AM ET, i.e., essentially Election Eve):**
- Proposition 41: 42% chance of passage (Yes 46¢, No 63¢... wait, that's odd. Yes 46¢ = 46%, No 63¢ = 63%. Hmm, they don't sum to 100 due to the spread. The headline says "42%" chance.)
- The Kalshi market dropped ~9.5 points in the last 24 hours
- Nijinn TruthIndex: 42.5% chance of passage (Kalshi only)
- On Point Politics forecast: Prop 41 "favored to fail" — Yes at 46.4%, only 20.4% chance to pass in their simulations
- NY Post (Oct 29): Kalshi 54% | Polymarket 59% — but this was several days before, and Kalshi has since dropped to ~42%
- Polymarket: ~66% Yes but with only $1,925 volume and huge bid/ask spread — unreliable, essentially illiquid

**Polling summary:**
| Poll | Dates | Yes | No | Result |
|------|-------|-----|-----|--------|
| Berkeley IGS | Aug 3-9 | 35% | 37% | No +2 |
| PPIC | Sept 4-10 | 51% | — | Yes leading |
| Berkeley IGS | Sept 15-20 | 37% | 33% | Yes +4 |
| IVC Media | Sept 23-28 | 49% | 36% | Yes +13 |
| PPIC | Oct 16-22 | 48% | 49% | No +1 (tied) |
| Berkeley IGS | Oct 19-25 | 38% | 47% | No +9 |

The trend is clearly deteriorating for Yes. Both of the final polls from the two most reputable California pollsters (PPIC and Berkeley IGS) show No leading.

**Key dynamics:**
1. The No side (SEIU-UHW, California Democratic Party, labor) has successfully framed Prop 41 as a "billionaire-funded trick" to undo the billionaire tax (Prop 40).
2. Major editorial boards oppose it.
3. California is a deep blue state where the Democratic Party and unions have strong messaging infrastructure.
4. Undecided voters (15-16% in the final IGS poll) typically break toward No on ballot initiatives.
5. Prediction markets have moved sharply toward No in the final days (Kalshi from 54% on Oct 29 to 42% by Nov 3).

**Counter-considerations:**
1. The Yes side has vastly more money ($58.4M vs $22.7M on Prop 41 specifically).
2. The ballot title sounds appealing (audits, accountability).
3. Prop 42 (the companion measure) has slightly better polling (51% yes in PPIC Oct).
4. Polymarket still shows ~66% Yes, but it's illiquid.

Weighing everything: The most reliable evidence — two independent, high-quality final polls showing No leading (especially Berkeley IGS at No +9), the sharp late movement in the Kalshi market toward No, and the On Point Politics forecast model giving Yes only a 20% chance — all point to the **No side being more likely to win**.

The polling average is around 43-46% Yes, which is below the 50% needed, and undecideds break toward No.

So the answer to "Which side is more likely to win?" is the No side → answer "no".

Let me do one more check on the very latest news to make sure I'm not missing anything (e.g., final weekend polls, early voting data).

- Polymarket: ~66% Yes but with only $1,925 in volume and a huge bid/ask spread (43%/89%) — illiquid and unreliable

**Other factors favoring No:**
- Undecided voters (15-16%) typically break 2:1 toward No on ballot initiatives
- The No campaign (SEIU-UHW, California Democratic Party, labor unions, Bernie Sanders) has framed it effectively as a "billionaire-funded trick"
- California is a deep-blue state; the measure's Yes vote "leans Republican" per On Point Politics
- Editorial boards (Mercury News, East Bay Times, LA Times, SF Chronicle) oppose it
- Support has been consistently declining through October as the opposition message lands

**Factors favoring Yes:**
- Massive spending advantage: $58.4M raised for Yes vs. $22.7M for No on Prop 41 specifically (billionaire-funded via Building a Better California, $103M spent supporting Prop 41)
- The ballot title/summary sounds appealing (audits, transparency, accountability)
- PPIC's October poll has it essentially tied (48-49)
- Prop 42 (companion) at 51% in PPIC October poll

**Weighing the evidence:**
The preponderance of evidence points to the No side being more likely to win:
1. Both final independent polls (PPIC Oct 16-22 and Berkeley IGS Oct 19-25) show No ahead
2. Clear downward trend in Yes support through the fall
3. Undecideds break toward No
4. The On Point Politics simulation model gives Yes just a 20.4% chance
5. Kalshi's final price (~42%) is below 50%, with sharp late movement toward No
6. Structural factors: Democratic-leaning electorate, measure's coalition leans Republican, strong editorial and party opposition

The one dissenting signal is the illiquid Polymarket market (~66% Yes, $1.9K volume), which is not credible given the tiny volume and wide spread. Also, the NY Post Oct 29 numbers (Kalshi 54%) were a few days older and Kalshi subsequently dropped ~12 points.

Note: One Mercury News article quotes the Yes campaign claiming "Recent polling shows that 58% support the concept of Prop 41" — this appears to be campaign spin about the "concept" (audits/accountability) rather than the actual ballot question.

So my conclusion: The **No** side is more likely to win. The answer to "Which side is more likely to win?" is "no" (i.e., the No side / the proposition is more likely to be defeated).

I now have a comprehensive picture. Let me summarize my research:

**Proposition 41 (California, Nov. 3, 2026 ballot):** A billionaire-funded counter-measure to Prop 40 (the "billionaire tax") that would prohibit new state taxes exempted from the spending limit and require audits of new special taxes. Yes = pass the measure; No = defeat it.

**Polling evidence (all public polls):**
- Berkeley IGS (Aug): Yes 35% / No 37%
- PPIC (Sept): Yes 51% / No 44%
- Berkeley IGS (mid-Sept): Yes 37% / No 33% (30% undecided)
- PPIC (Oct 16–22): Yes 48% / No 49% — tied/tilted No
- Berkeley IGS (Oct 19–25): Yes 38% / No 47% — No +9, with 16% undecided

Both final, high-quality polls show the No side ahead, and Yes support has steadily eroded through October as the "billionaire-funded trick" message landed.

**Forecasts & markets:**
- On Point Politics model (Nov 2): Yes at 46.4%, only a **20.4% chance to pass** — "favored to fail"
- Kalshi (Election Eve): ~42% chance of passage, having dropped ~9.5 points in the final 24 hours
- Polymarket showed ~66% Yes, but with only ~$1.9K volume and a 43¢/89¢ bid-ask spread — too illiquid to be meaningful

**Other factors:** Undecided voters historically break toward No on California initiatives; the Democratic Party, labor unions, and major editorial boards all oppose it in a deep-blue state; and the Yes coalition leans Republican in a Democratic-trending midterm electorate. The Yes side's massive spending advantage ($58M vs. $23M) hasn't stopped the slide.

The weight of evidence — both final polls showing No ahead, a deteriorating trend, undecideds breaking No, a forecast model giving Yes only ~20%, and Kalshi falling below 50% — indicates the **No side** is more likely to win.
